title: The Queen's Trial
subtitle: Caroline of Brunswick and the Bill of Pains and Penalties, House of Lords, London, 1820–1821
intro: On 5 June 1820 Caroline of Brunswick landed at Dover to claim her place as Queen. Her husband, newly King George IV, had lived apart from her for almost twenty-five years and wanted her neither crowned nor prayed for. The next day he sent Parliament two green bags of evidence gathered by a commission in Milan, and by July Lord Liverpool's reluctant government had brought in a Bill of Pains and Penalties to strip her of her title and dissolve the marriage by Act of Parliament.

It was not formally a trial, and that was the Queen's first complaint. But from 17 August to 10 November the House of Lords sat as a court: the Crown's law officers called Italian servants to swear to her adultery with her chamberlain Bartolomeo Pergami, and her counsel, Henry Brougham and Thomas Denman, cross-examined, called their own witnesses and summed up. The peers then voted, and when the third reading passed by only nine the government let the bill die. Eight months later she was turned away from the coronation; three weeks after that she was dead.

The court's own record is here first: the Lords' Minutes of Evidence and Hansard's reports, close to verbatim for the witnesses, reported for the speeches. Beside it stand the people who wrote the case down as it happened. Caroline's own voice survives mostly in letters that others drafted, notably the open letter of 7 August 1820 generally credited to Cobbett, and in last words reported by Brougham. The King's survives in a formal message and in private letters. The witness Majocchi speaks only through interpreters, yet his 'non mi ricordo' became the most quoted phrase of the year.

Outside the chamber, the Whig Thomas Creevey wrote to his stepdaughter almost daily from the gallery; the courtier Charles Greville kept his diary; W. H. Fremantle reported to the Marquess of Buckingham from beside the King's lodge at Windsor; Robert Plumer Ward kept a government man's diary; Harriet Arbuthnot heard from Wellington what passed in Cabinet; and Princess Lieven wrote to Metternich from the King's Pavilion at Brighton. The radical press, Cobbett's Register and William Hone's pamphlets, turned the evidence into weekly argument and cheap satire for a crowd that marched in its tens of thousands and signed addresses in numbers never seen before.

The honest record is therefore mostly letters, an official transcript and printed pamphlets, with a few diaries. Every one of these writers took a side, and the question the Lords were asked, whether the Queen had committed adultery, was never decided: the bill was abandoned, not voted down on the evidence. This chapter sets out what each side said and recorded, and leaves that question where the House of Lords left it.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian; Britain had used the Gregorian calendar since 1752. Days of the week are given from the calendar. Where a letter or diary is dated only by month, or covers several days, it is shown with range or month precision and marked approximate.

eyes.name: House of Lords: Journals, Minutes of Evidence and Hansard
eyes.role: The official and semi-official record of the proceedings on the Bill of Pains and Penalties, with Lord Liverpool, the Prime Minister, as the bill's mover and the peers sitting as both legislators and judges
eyes.side: Parliament; the Crown's prosecution (Attorney General Gifford, Solicitor General Copley) and the Queen's counsel both recorded
eyes.where: The House of Lords chamber, Westminster
eyes.form: official record (minutes of evidence; reporters' debates)
eyes.language: English; Italian answers rendered through sworn interpreters
eyes.authenticity: The Lords printed the Minutes of Evidence taken on the second reading as an official folio. Hansard's Parliamentary Debates (vols 2–3, 1820) reprinted the questions and answers and the speeches from reporters' notes; spellings of witness names vary (Hansard prints 'Majoochi'). It is close to verbatim for the evidence, less so for speeches.
eyes.bio: Not a person but the voice of the proceeding itself. A bill, not a trial, was the chosen form: if passed it would have stripped Caroline of her title and dissolved the marriage by Act of Parliament, so the peers heard counsel and witnesses as if in court and then voted as legislators.

sources.title: Hansard, House of Lords, 22 August 1820 (Majocchi examined)
Hansard, House of Lords, 7 September 1820 (summing up)
Royal Collection: Minutes of Evidence taken on the second reading of the Bill

eyes.name: Caroline of Brunswick, Queen of the United Kingdom
eyes.role: Queen consort from January 1820, aged 52; separated from George since 1796 and living in Italy since 1814; the accused
eyes.side: The Queen's party: Whig counsel, radicals, the London crowd
eyes.where: Landed at Dover 5 June 1820; lodged in South Audley Street, then Brandenburgh House, Hammersmith; attended the Lords through the hearing
eyes.form: dated letter; words reported by others
eyes.language: English (her letters were often drafted by advisers)
eyes.authenticity: Her open letter to the King dated 7 August 1820 was printed in The Times and widely reprinted; the radical William Cobbett is generally thought to have composed it, so it is her voice through another pen. Her last words survive only as reported by Brougham to Creevey.
eyes.bio: A German princess married in 1795 to a prince who had already secretly married Maria Fitzherbert, she lived apart from him for most of their marriage. Her decision to come home and claim her place as Queen in 1820 turned a royal quarrel into the largest popular movement of the decade.

sources.title: Royal Collection Trust, Treasures from the Royal Archives (letter of 7 August 1820)
Yale Law Library, Trial by Media: The Queen Caroline Affair

eyes.name: George IV
eyes.role: King from 29 January 1820, aged 57; the petitioner in all but name, pressing ministers for a divorce
eyes.where: Carlton House and the Royal Lodge, Windsor Great Park; Brighton
eyes.vantage_label: the King who wanted the marriage ended
eyes.authenticity: His message of 6 June 1820 is in the Parliamentary Archives (HL/PO/JO/10/8/512, no. 218). His private letters were edited by A. Aspinall (The Letters of King George IV, 1938); they are used here only in digest.
eyes.bio: He never appeared at the hearing and stayed largely out of sight while ministers carried a case they had not wanted. His letters show a man following the evidence day by day and raging at the defence witnesses.

sources.title: UK Parliament Living Heritage: Message from the King, 6 June 1820

eyes.name: Henry Brougham
eyes.role: Whig MP, aged 42; the Queen's Attorney General and leading counsel
eyes.where: At the bar of the House of Lords; Brougham Hall, Westmorland, during the September adjournment
eyes.authenticity: His speeches survive in Hansard's reporters' text; his letters to Creevey are printed in The Creevey Papers (ed. Sir Herbert Maxwell, 1903).
eyes.bio: Ambitious, brilliant and mistrusted by his own allies, Brougham had advised Caroline for years and met her in France on her way home. His cross-examinations broke the Crown's Italian witnesses, and the case made him a popular hero; he became Lord Chancellor in 1830.

sources.title: Hansard, House of Lords, 3 October 1820: Defence of Her Majesty
Hansard: Mr Henry Brougham, 1820 contributions

eyes.name: Thomas Denman
eyes.role: Whig MP and barrister, aged 41; the Queen's Solicitor General
eyes.where: At the bar of the House of Lords
eyes.authenticity: His summing-up of 24–25 October 1820 survives in Hansard's reported text. The line most remembered from it, his use of 'Go, and sin no more', is best known through the lampoons that followed and is treated here as reported rather than checked against the text.
eyes.bio: Denman was the more emotional of the Queen's two counsel. His closing speech attacked the prosecution witnesses as perjured and compared the King's treatment of his wife to Nero's of Octavia, which the King did not forgive; Denman later became Lord Chief Justice.

sources.title: Hansard, House of Lords, 24 October 1820: Summing up

eyes.name: Teodoro (Theodore) Majocchi
eyes.role: Former servant in Caroline's household in Italy; the Crown's first witness
eyes.where: Witness box at the bar of the House of Lords
eyes.authenticity: His words survive only as interpreted into English and printed in the Minutes of Evidence and Hansard (as 'Majoochi'). The famous 'Non mi ricordo' is in that record: counsel asked that his answer be put to the House as 'I do not remember'.
eyes.bio: He had served the Princess and her chamberlain Bartolomeo Pergami on her travels and was brought to London with other Italian witnesses gathered by the Milan Commission. His confident evidence in chief and his repeated failures of memory under Brougham made him the trial's most famous figure and a byword in the streets.

sources.title: Hansard, House of Lords, 22 August 1820
National Portrait Gallery, Regency Portraits Catalogue: Theodore Majocchi

eyes.name: Thomas Creevey
eyes.role: Whig politician and gossip, aged 52, returned for Appleby in 1820; a daily spectator in the Lords
eyes.side: Whig opposition; hostile to the bill
eyes.where: House of Lords and Brooks's Club, London; Knowsley in August 1820
eyes.form: dated letters (to his stepdaughter Elizabeth Ord) and journal notes
eyes.authenticity: Edited by Sir Herbert Maxwell as The Creevey Papers (1903), from the manuscripts later held in Northumberland. Maxwell selected and sometimes trimmed; letter dates are Creevey's own headings.
eyes.bio: Creevey wrote to Miss Ord almost daily from the Lords, often while the evidence was still being given. He disliked both King and Queen, which makes his running score of the case, and of Brougham, sharper than a partisan's.

sources.title: The Creevey Papers (1903), Internet Archive text
Northumberland Archives: The Creevey Papers

eyes.name: Charles Cavendish Fulke Greville
eyes.role: Aged 25; secretary to Earl Bathurst and holder of the reversion of the Clerkship of the Privy Council; racing man
eyes.side: Tory-leaning courtier, sceptical of the bill
eyes.where: London and the Lords; Oatlands (the Duke of York's house) and Newmarket
eyes.authenticity: The journal was published by Henry Reeve in 1874, with names and passages suppressed; later editions restored some cuts. Entries are cited here from the 1874 text as reproduced online.
eyes.bio: Well placed in the Duke of York's circle and later famous as the diarist of three reigns, Greville watched the affair as an insider who found it both absorbing and disgraceful. He attended the hearing daily in October.

sources.title: The Greville Memoirs, chapter I (1820), historyhome.co.uk
The Greville Memoirs (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: William Henry Fremantle
eyes.role: Grenvillite MP, aged 54, political agent of the Marquess of Buckingham
eyes.side: The Grenvillites, a small group between Government and Whigs
eyes.where: Englefield Green, near the King's Royal Lodge; London; Brighton
eyes.authenticity: Printed in the Duke of Buckingham and Chandos, Memoirs of the Court of George IV, 1820–1830 (1859), from family papers; the editor linked letters with his own commentary.
eyes.bio: Fremantle's letters to Buckingham are a running report from a man who lived beside Windsor Great Park and heard what the King's household said. He reads the trial as a problem of order and of who would form the next government.

sources.title: Memoirs of the Court of George IV, vol. 1 (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: Robert Plumer Ward
eyes.role: Tory MP and office-holder, aged 55; novelist
eyes.authenticity: Extracts from his diary were published by Edmund Phipps (1850) and quoted in Buckingham's Memoirs of the Court of George IV (1859); only those printed extracts are used.
eyes.bio: A loyal ministerialist, Ward recorded the weakness he saw on every side as the bill came to its final votes. His diary gives the government's own view of the night it gave up.

sources.title: Memoirs of the Court of George IV, vol. 1 (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: William Hone
eyes.role: Radical bookseller and satirist, aged 40, of Ludgate Hill; acquitted of blasphemous libel in 1817
eyes.where: His shop at 45 Ludgate Hill, London
eyes.authenticity: The pamphlets survive in many copies and editions; George Cruikshank cut the wood engravings. Exact days of publication are not always printed, so dates are given to the year or season.
eyes.bio: Hone turned the trial into cheap print that sold in tens of thousands. His squib 'Non mi ricordo!' took Majocchi's answer and put it in the King's mouth.

sources.title: Morgan Library: 'Non mi ricordo!' (Cruikshank, 1820)
William Hone: An Annotated Bibliography

eyes.name: William Cobbett
eyes.role: Radical journalist, aged 57, editor of the Weekly Political Register
eyes.side: Radical press; adviser to the Queen
eyes.authenticity: The Register is fully preserved. His authorship of the Queen's letter of 7 August 1820 rests on his own later claims and on scholarship; it is a strong attribution, not a signature.
eyes.bio: Cobbett saw the Queen's cause as a lever against the whole system of 'Old Corruption'. He wrote for her as well as about her, so in this chapter his pen appears on both sides of the page.

sources.title: 'The Queen Caroline Affair in Radical Periodicals', Culture (De Gruyter, 2022)

eyes.name: Harriet Arbuthnot
eyes.role: Tory political hostess, aged 26, wife of the Treasury Secretary Charles Arbuthnot and confidante of the Duke of Wellington
eyes.authenticity: First published 1950 (ed. F. Bamford and the 7th Duke of Wellington), so used here in digest only.
eyes.bio: Her journal opens in 1820 just as the King demanded a divorce, and Wellington told her what passed in Cabinet. It shows the crisis from inside the government before Caroline ever landed.

sources.title: The Diary Junction: Harriet Arbuthnot

eyes.name: Dorothea, Princess Lieven
eyes.role: Wife of the Russian ambassador, aged 35; intimate of the King's circle
eyes.side: Diplomatic corps; the King's social world
eyes.where: London and the Royal Pavilion, Brighton
eyes.authenticity: Her letters to Metternich were returned to her in 1827 and published in English translation in 1937 (ed. Peter Quennell); digest only.
eyes.bio: Lieven wrote to Metternich in Vienna as the King's guest and observer. Her letters of the trial months dwell on the King's world, its gossip and its cost, at the very time the Queen's counsel were attacking it.

sources.title: Brighton & Hove Museums: Dorothea von Lieven, letter-writer at George's court

entries.headline: 'Non mi ricordo!' turns the witness's words on the King
entries.digest: Hone published a squib titled with Majocchi's answer, with Cruikshank's woodcut of the King as a bloated dandy at the bar of a court. In it the King himself answers his examiner with the witness's helpless refrain. It joined Hone's 'The Queen's Matrimonial Ladder' among the best-selling prints of the year.
entries.source_note: Morgan Library, 'Non mi ricordo!' (title woodcut, printed by and for William Hone, 1820). Day of publication not established.

entries.headline: Wellington: the King will sack his ministers without a divorce
entries.digest: Ten days into the new reign, Wellington told Harriet Arbuthnot that the King meant to dismiss his ministers unless they undertook to get him a divorce. The Cabinet had refused, and she noted that the Whigs would vote solidly against any divorce. The whole trial is already here in outline, months before Caroline set out for England.
entries.source_note: Journal of Mrs Arbuthnot (1950), entry 9 Feb 1820, as summarised by The Diary Junction.

entries.headline: The King will not let the Queen be prayed for
entries.digest: Greville heard that the Cabinet had sat until two in the morning. The King refused, again and again, to allow the Queen's name into the revised prayers of the Church, and nothing would move him. The question of the Liturgy would become one of the Queen's grievances and one of the crowd's slogans.
entries.source_note: Greville Memoirs (1874), ch. I, entry 14 Feb 1820, historyhome.co.uk.

entries.headline: Brougham gone to meet her; no one knows her intent
entries.digest: Writing from the Duke of York's house, Greville recorded that the Queen was on her way and that Brougham had gone to meet her on the coast of France. No one in the King's circle knew what she meant to do, and Greville set down the King's behaviour at Ascot as the news came in.
entries.source_note: Greville Memoirs (1874), entry 4 June 1820.

entries.headline: The King sends his green bags to Parliament
entries.digest: The day after Caroline landed at Dover, the King sent a message to both Houses with sealed green bags of papers on her conduct abroad. He asked the Lords to give her conduct since leaving the kingdom their immediate and serious attention. It was the formal opening of the case against her.
entries.source_note: Message from the King, Parliamentary Archives HL/PO/JO/10/8/512 no. 218 (UK Parliament Living Heritage).

entries.headline: Riding out to see the Queen come in
entries.digest: Greville rode out on the Greenwich road to watch the Queen's entry into London. The crowds were enormous and wild with enthusiasm, and the radical Alderman Matthew Wood sat beside her in the open carriage. He closed the entry with the question everyone was asking.
entries.quote: What will be done next? How is it to end?
entries.source_note: Greville Memoirs (1874), entry 7 June 1820.

entries.headline: The Register takes up the Queen's cause
entries.digest: Within days of her landing Cobbett's Political Register carried its first article on the affair, addressed to the reformers. He presented the Queen's wrongs as one more face of the corrupt system the radicals were fighting, and from then on the paper became one of her loudest voices.
entries.source_note: Dating from 'The Queen Caroline Affair in Radical Periodicals', Culture (De Gruyter, 2022); content summarised from that study.

entries.headline: Guardsmen cheer the Queen
entries.digest: Greville recorded that a battalion of the 3rd Guards had been disciplined after refusing to give up their ball cartridges, and that drunken soldiers had been heard cheering the Queen in the streets. To a courtier this was the most frightening sign of all: the army itself seemed unsure.
entries.source_note: Greville Memoirs (1874), entry 16 June 1820.

entries.headline: Counsel at the bar; Wilberforce jeered
entries.digest: Against expectation the Queen's counsel were heard at the bar of the Lords, Brougham powerfully and Denman with an admired opening. Outside, a crowd abused William Wilberforce, who had tried to broker a compromise, calling him after the hypocrite in a popular play.
entries.source_note: Greville Memoirs (1874), entry 27 June 1820.

entries.headline: Liverpool brings in the Bill of Pains and Penalties
entries.digest: After a secret committee of peers reported on the green bags, Lord Liverpool introduced a bill to deprive Caroline of the title and rights of Queen and to dissolve her marriage. It charged an adulterous connection with Bartolomeo Pergami, her Italian chamberlain. The bill was read a first time and the hearing of evidence fixed for August.
entries.source_note: Lords Journals and Hansard, 5 July 1820; dating confirmed by the Wikipedia article on the bill and the De Gruyter study.

entries.headline: Opinion turns; the soldiers restless
entries.digest: After the committee's report Greville found the mood had swung: most people now expected the charges to be proved and the King to get his divorce. Yet the troops in London were showing discontent, and he recorded Henry Luttrell's dry joke about where that might lead.
entries.source_note: Greville Memoirs (1874), entry 6 July 1820.

entries.headline: The City is with her
entries.digest: Fremantle told Buckingham that London was quieter but gloomier. The Queen's support in the City was growing, the press and some of the alehouses were openly for her, and the Lords' hearing was expected to begin on 17 August.
entries.quote: The City is completely with her
entries.source_note: Buckingham, Memoirs of the Court of George IV (1859), vol. 1, letter of 19 July 1820.

entries.headline: A public letter to Lord Liverpool
entries.digest: Cobbett used his Register to address the Prime Minister directly, attacking the proceeding as a political persecution dressed up as law. The open letter to a minister was his favourite weapon, and this one was timed for the eve of the hearing.
entries.source_note: Dating from 'The Queen Caroline Affair in Radical Periodicals', Culture (De Gruyter, 2022); content in outline only.

entries.headline: The Queen writes to the King
entries.digest: In a long open letter to her husband, Caroline reviewed a quarter century of ill-treatment, from her separation to the loss of her daughter, and protested at being tried by a bill instead of in a court of law. She warned him that the proceeding threatened the stability of his own throne. The letter appeared in The Times and was reprinted across the country; Cobbett is generally thought to have drafted it.
entries.quote: sent me sorrowing through the World
entries.source_note: Royal Collection Trust (RA GEO/BOX/13/83 exhibition text); Yale Law Library 'Trial by Media'.

entries.headline: Nothing to choose between them
entries.digest: Staying with Lord Derby, Creevey gave Miss Ord his view of the Queen's case on the eve of the hearing. He had no illusions about either party to the marriage and thought there was nothing to choose between King and Queen.
entries.quote: not a pin to chuse between them
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), letter of 7 Aug 1820.

entries.headline: The King in hiding at Windsor
entries.digest: From his house beside Windsor Great Park, Fremantle reported that the King was living in seclusion with Lady Conyngham. Everyone was waiting to see how King and ministers would answer the Queen's letter.
entries.source_note: Buckingham, Memoirs of the Court of George IV (1859), vol. 1, letter of 11 Aug 1820.

entries.headline: The hearing opens; a motion to drop it fails
entries.digest: With the peers called over and the Queen present, the House began the second-reading hearing. The Duke of Leinster's motion to throw the bill out at once was defeated by 206 votes to 41, and Brougham and Denman opened with objections to the whole procedure.
entries.source_note: Hansard HL 17 Aug 1820; division figures also in Creevey's letter of that day.

entries.headline: The Queen's entrance, described from the gallery
entries.digest: Creevey wrote to Miss Ord from inside the Lords as the hearing began. He described the Queen's entrance, her veil hiding most of her face, and likened her bobbing curtsies to a Dutch toy that always rights itself. He also noted the poor reception of the Duke of York's remarks.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), letter headed House of Lords, 17 Aug 1820.

entries.headline: The Attorney General opens the Crown's case
entries.digest: Sir Robert Gifford set out the charges: that the Princess had lived in adultery with Pergami across Italy, Sicily and the eastern Mediterranean, at Naples, on a polacca at sea and at her villa on Lake Como. He promised that servants who had seen it would prove it.
entries.source_note: Hansard HL 19 Aug 1820; Wikipedia, Pains and Penalties Bill 1820.

entries.headline: First witness; the Queen walks out
entries.digest: Gifford finished his opening and called the first witness, the former servant Majocchi. When he appeared at the bar the Queen rose and left the chamber. He gave his evidence in chief in Italian through the Crown's interpreter, describing the sleeping arrangements on the Princess's travels.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia (Pains and Penalties Bill 1820), citing the Lords record of 21 Aug 1820.

entries.headline: 'Non mi ricordo' under cross-examination
entries.digest: Majocchi finished his evidence in chief, telling the Solicitor General that the Princess took breakfast with Pergami. Then Brougham cross-examined him, and on point after point he answered that he did not know or did not remember. Brougham had the interpreters state exactly what 'non mi ricordo' meant so the peers would hear it as 'I do not remember'.
entries.quote: I do not know; I do not remember.
entries.source_note: Hansard HL 22 Aug 1820, vol. 2 cc837–69 (witness printed as 'Majoochi').

entries.headline: Brougham wins freedom to cross-examine
entries.digest: Creevey reported that Lord Harrowby's motion allowing Brougham to cross-examine without restriction had carried by 121 to 106. He read the narrow vote as a sign of the peers' unease with the Crown's case.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), entry of 29 Aug 1820.

entries.headline: The lady's maid's letters undo her
entries.digest: Louise Demont, the Queen's former maid and one of the Crown's key witnesses, was cross-examined over two days. Creevey watched the prosecution suffer as letters she had written praising her mistress were put to her and she admitted they were hers.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), letters of 1–2 Sept 1820.

entries.headline: The Solicitor General sums up for the Crown
entries.digest: Sir John Copley summed up the evidence for the prosecution, asking the peers to set the servants' consistent testimony against the defence's attacks on their character. The House then prepared to adjourn so the Queen's counsel could gather witnesses.
entries.source_note: Hansard HL 7 Sept 1820, 'Summing up', vol. 2 cc1345–92.

entries.headline: Adjourned to October; peers angry
entries.digest: The Lords adjourned the hearing to 3 October. Creevey reported the peers' irritation at being held in town through the autumn and the talk that the divorce clause might be dropped to save the bill.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), letters of 7–9 Sept 1820.

entries.headline: Punished for praying for the Queen
entries.digest: From home in the north, Brougham sent Creevey two stories of the country's divisions: a Scottish kirk session and a Yeomanry chaplain had both been penalised for praying for the Queen. The prayers question had reached the parishes.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), Brougham to Creevey, 14 Sept 1820.

entries.headline: It may come down to the troops
entries.digest: Fremantle expected rioting if the bill went forward and doubted it could pass. The Duke of York, bitterly hostile to the Queen, had said the army would be relied on and troops posted at the approaches to Parliament if needed; the government seemed alarmed.
entries.quote: it must eventually depend upon the troops
entries.source_note: Buckingham, Memoirs of the Court of George IV (1859), vol. 1, letter of 27 Sept 1820.

entries.headline: The King rails at the defence witnesses
entries.digest: Following the evidence from a distance, the King wrote that he had never expected to live to see so much prevarication and lying as the defence case produced. His letters of these weeks show how closely he tracked each day's testimony.
entries.source_note: Letters of King George IV, ed. A. Aspinall (1938), p. 371, as cited in Jane Robins, The Trial of Queen Caroline (2006/07); exact day not checked.

entries.headline: Brougham opens the defence
entries.digest: Brougham began by asking the peers' indulgence, then went through the Crown's case place by place to show what the Attorney General had promised and the witnesses had failed to prove. He argued the Italian witnesses had been paid and drilled at Milan, and that Majocchi remembered everything useful and nothing awkward. Lovers as reckless as the story required were, he said, simply improbable.
entries.quote: guilt was wary, and innocence alone unwary
entries.source_note: Hansard HL 3 Oct 1820, 'Defence of Her Majesty', vol. 3 cc112–78.

entries.headline: The peroration: save the country
entries.digest: Resuming next morning, Brougham finished his speech with an appeal to the peers to reject the bill for the sake of the Crown, the Church and the country itself. Contemporaries ranked it among the greatest speeches of the age; the defence witnesses followed.
entries.source_note: Hansard HL 4 Oct 1820 (text not fetched); continuation confirmed by the adjournment order at the end of the 3 Oct record and by Creevey's letters of 3–4 Oct.

entries.headline: 'As good as I expected'
entries.digest: Creevey followed Brougham's speech across the two days and gave Miss Ord a measured verdict: it was as good as he had hoped, which for Creevey, who mistrusted Brougham, was high praise.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), letters of 3–4 Oct 1820.

entries.headline: The finest oratory in years
entries.digest: Greville called Brougham's speech the most magnificent display of argument and oratory in many years; even hostile peers such as Lord Lonsdale were impressed. He now expected the bill to be thrown out and the ministers to fall, while London stayed in uproar.
entries.source_note: Greville Memoirs (1874), entry 8 Oct 1820.

entries.headline: Every day in the gallery
entries.digest: Attending daily, Greville found that Lieutenant Hownam's evidence for the defence had convinced many that the adultery was in fact proved, though the bill's opponents disputed it. He saw ministers running the case like a military campaign, and judged their sending away of the witness Rastelli a rash blunder that had turned against them.
entries.source_note: Greville Memoirs (1874), entry 15 Oct 1820.

entries.headline: Denman: the Queen is the victim of perjury
entries.digest: Denman began his summing-up for the Queen by taking apart the Naples story the Attorney General had opened with. He called Louise Demont the most dangerous witness because she built falsehood on a base of truth, and told the peers that the Queen was the victim of a conspiracy.
entries.quote: the victim of perjury and conspiracy
entries.source_note: Hansard HL 24 Oct 1820, 'Summing up', vol. 3 cc1027–95.

entries.headline: Nero, Octavia, and 'go and sin no more'
entries.digest: Denman closed by comparing the King's treatment of his wife to Nero's of Octavia, a barb the King never forgot. He ended with Christ's words to the woman taken in adultery, which seemed to concede guilt and was mocked in verse and print for weeks after.
entries.source_note: Creevey (letters of 21–24 Oct 1820) praises the Nero and Octavia passage; the closing scripture and its mockery are reported in later accounts. Day of the close not checked against Hansard.

entries.headline: The dragon chandelier and the King's whims
entries.digest: While the Queen's counsel were attacking the King's character in the Lords, Lieven wrote to Metternich about the Pavilion. She marvelled at the dragon chandelier in the Banqueting Room, which she put at £11,000, and at the jumble of styles in a building she reckoned had cost £700,000. The letter does not mention the Queen at all.
entries.source_note: Brighton & Hove Museums, 'Dorothea von Lieven' (cites letter of 27 Oct 1820; the museum notes the chandelier actually cost £5,613).

entries.headline: The brass founders march
entries.digest: As the peers counted heads for the coming votes, Creevey described a huge procession of the brass founders carrying addresses to the Queen. Trade after trade was marching to Hammersmith that autumn.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), letter of 30 Oct 1820.

entries.headline: Second reading carried by 28
entries.digest: After the peers' own debate, led for the bill by Lord Eldon and against it by Lord Grey, the second reading passed by 123 votes to 95. The majority was far below what the government needed to face the Commons.
entries.source_note: Hansard HL 6 Nov 1820; figures confirmed in Creevey's letters and the Wikipedia article.

entries.headline: Third reading by nine; Liverpool gives up
entries.digest: The third reading was carried by only 108 to 99. Lord Liverpool then told the House that with so narrow a majority the government would not proceed, and moved that the bill be read again in six months, the parliamentary form for killing it.
entries.source_note: Hansard HL 10 Nov 1820; Plumer Ward's diary and Creevey's letter of the same day.

entries.headline: The government's diarist records the climb-down
entries.digest: Ward noted the division of 108 to 99, a majority of nine, and Liverpool's withdrawal of the bill. Days earlier he had written of weakness and bad conduct on every side; now it was over without a verdict.
entries.source_note: Plumer Ward's diary for 2 and 10 Nov 1820, as printed in Buckingham, Memoirs of the Court of George IV (1859).

entries.headline: Eldon's lone 'Not content'
entries.digest: Creevey described the scene when Liverpool moved to put the bill off: the Lord Chancellor Eldon's audible 'Not content', the Duke of Clarence shouting 'Content', and the confusion of a House undoing its own work.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), letter headed Brooks's, 10 Nov 1820.

entries.headline: The Lords have nearly ruined themselves
entries.digest: The morning after, Creevey summed up for Miss Ord. The bill was dead, and he thought the peers' conduct through the whole affair had come close to ruining the character of their House. London was preparing illuminations.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), letter of 11 Nov 1820.

entries.headline: Black Rod cuts Denman off
entries.digest: When Parliament met, Denman rose in the Commons to read a message from the Queen and was interrupted by Black Rod summoning members to the Lords for the prorogation. Creevey described the uproar and the session closed without even a speech from the throne.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), letter of 23 Nov 1820; Phillimore's letter of the same day in Buckingham's Memoirs agrees.

entries.headline: The King talks four hours with Grenville
entries.digest: Fremantle reported that the King had sent for Lord Grenville and talked with him from eleven until three, low before dinner and cheerful after. With the bill gone, the question at Windsor was whether the King would change his ministers.
entries.source_note: Buckingham, Memoirs of the Court of George IV (1859), vol. 1, letter of 26 Nov 1820.

entries.headline: Dinner with the Queen
entries.digest: Creevey dined with Caroline at Brandenburgh House and described the house by the river, her manner at table and her guests. The Queen of the crowds was by now an uncertain host, short of money and of allies.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), entry of 11 Feb 1821.

entries.headline: Turned away at every door of the Abbey
entries.digest: On coronation morning Brougham wrote to Creevey that the Queen had left Brandenburgh House early and been refused entry at each door of Westminster Abbey she tried. On her way back the crowd mostly cheered her, while the King's procession met hisses mixed with cheers.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), Brougham to Creevey, 19 July 1821.

entries.headline: 'I am going to die'
entries.digest: Creevey passed on Brougham's account of the Queen's last illness: she had signed her will and told Brougham plainly that she was dying. Lord Hood's letter from Brandenburgh House gave the hour of her death the night before, 7 August.
entries.quote: I am going to die, Mr. Brougham
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), letters of 8 Aug 1821 (Creevey to Miss Ord; Hood to Brougham).

entries.headline: Did Brougham serve her well?
entries.digest: Three days after her death Creevey let his old suspicion show: he thought Brougham had harmed the Queen by his conduct before the trial. He also recorded her wish to leave jewels to her servant Victorine, which Brougham had brushed aside.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), letter of 11 Aug 1821.

entries.headline: Fighting the government's haste over the funeral
entries.digest: On the day the coffin left Hammersmith for Harwich and burial in Brunswick, Brougham wrote that he and Stephen Lushington had protested at the speed the government imposed on the funeral. The route, chosen to avoid the City, was blocked by crowds that day.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), Brougham to Creevey, 14 Aug 1821; route from pasttense.co.uk.

entries.headline: Two dead on the funeral route
entries.digest: Creevey reported the clash at the funeral, when Life Guards fired on the crowd and two men were killed. He noted the inquest's verdict of wilful murder against soldiers of the Life Guards, though no one was named.
entries.source_note: Creevey Papers (1903), letter of 28 Sept 1821 enclosing Sefton's of 13 Sept.

claims.claim: The King's message asks the Lords to examine the Queen's conduct abroad, with sealed green bags of evidence.
Bill introduced to strip Caroline of her title and dissolve the marriage, charging adultery with Bartolomeo Pergami.
The Queen protests that she is tried by bill, not in a court of law, and warns of danger to the throne.
claims.evidence: Open letter to the King, printed in The Times; RCT and Yale Law Library

claims.claim: Attorney General Gifford opens: adulterous intercourse with Pergami across Italy and at sea, to be proved by servants.
Majocchi testifies the Princess breakfasted with Pergami; under cross-examination repeatedly cannot remember.
Louise Demont's own letters praising the Queen damage the prosecution under cross-examination.
Solicitor General Copley sums up the Crown's evidence.
Defence argues the Italian witnesses were paid and coached at Milan and the Crown's opening promises went unproved.
claims.evidence: Hansard HL 3 Oct 1820, 'Defence of Her Majesty'

claims.claim: The King writes that the defence case is full of prevarication and lying.
claims.evidence: Aspinall, Letters of King George IV (1938), p. 371, as cited by Robins

claims.claim: Denman sums up: the Queen is the victim of perjury and conspiracy; Demont builds falsehood on truth.
'Non mi ricordo!' puts the witness's refrain into the King's mouth.
claims.evidence: Morgan Library copy of the title woodcut (Hone/Cruikshank, 1820)

claims.claim: Third reading carried 108 to 99; Liverpool withdraws the bill (to be read in six months).
A government supporter records the majority of nine and the withdrawal.
claims.evidence: Plumer Ward's diary, printed in Buckingham's Memoirs (1859)

claims.claim: The Queen is refused admission at every door of Westminster Abbey on coronation day.
claims.evidence: Brougham to Creevey, 19 July 1821, Creevey Papers (1903)

claims.claim: Inquest returns wilful murder against Life Guards for a death on the funeral route.

convergences.label: The Queen enters London; the King's green bags reach Parliament
convergences.note: On the same day the King's formal message asked the Lords to judge his wife, Greville was riding out to watch the crowds cheer her in. The legal case and the street case began together.

convergences.label: The Queen's open letter to the King
convergences.note: Caroline's letter, probably in Cobbett's words, cast her as a wronged wife denied a fair court; that same day Creevey, at Knowsley, thought neither spouse deserved sympathy. Radical pen, royal signature and Whig shrug in one day.

convergences.label: The hearing opens in the Lords
convergences.note: The record gives the division of 206 to 41 against dropping the bill; Creevey, writing in the House, gives the Queen's veil, her curtsies and the peers' mood, which the record leaves out.

convergences.label: Majocchi under cross-examination
convergences.note: The record preserves the witness's 'I do not remember' and the interpreters' argument over its meaning; Brougham built his defence on it; within weeks Hone had made it the catchphrase of the season.

convergences.label: Brougham's defence speech (3–4 October)
convergences.note: The Hansard text gives the argument; Creevey, sceptical of Brougham, grants it was as good as expected; Greville, no Whig, calls it the finest oratory in years and expects the bill to fall.

convergences.label: Denman sums up for the Queen
convergences.note: In the Lords Denman called the Queen the victim of perjury and likened the King to Nero, a passage Creevey singled out for praise; that week Lieven was writing about the King's chandeliers at Brighton, and the King was writing of the defence's lies.

convergences.label: The bill is abandoned
convergences.note: The record gives 108 to 99 and Liverpool's motion; the government man records it flatly; the Whig records Eldon's lone 'Not content' and a House undoing itself.

convergences.label: The Queen's death (7 August 1821) and its news
convergences.note: Brougham, at Brandenburgh House, carried her last words; Creevey passed them on and within days was doubting whether Brougham had served her well.

ties.note: Brougham wrote to Creevey through the trial and its aftermath, and Creevey's letters to Miss Ord retail and judge what Brougham told him.
Brougham cross-examined Majocchi on 22 August 1820, and the 'Non mi ricordo' answers he drew out became the centre of his defence.
Co-counsel for the Queen: Brougham opened the defence, Denman summed it up.
Husband and wife since 1795, separated since 1796; he sought the divorce, she was the accused.
Cobbett is generally credited with drafting the Queen's open letter of 7 August 1820 and some of her replies to addresses.
Hone's pamphlet 'Non mi ricordo!' took its title from Majocchi's answers in the Lords.
Fremantle wrote from Englefield Green beside the Royal Lodge, reporting what the King's household said and did.
Lieven was a frequent guest of the King at Brighton and wrote to Metternich from the Pavilion during the trial.
Denman's comparison of the King to Nero in the Lords left a lasting royal resentment.
Both Tory insiders recorded the King's divorce ultimatum to the Cabinet in February 1820, from Wellington's side and from the Duke of York's.
Both men's words reached print in the same compilation, Buckingham's Memoirs of the Court of George IV (1859).

threads_out.note: Caroline's father, Charles William Ferdinand, Duke of Brunswick, commanded the allied army in 1792 and gave his name to the Brunswick Manifesto threatening Paris, a document that hardened the Revolution against the monarchy.

Lord Castlereagh, Britain's plenipotentiary at the Congress of Vienna, led for the government in the Commons through the Queen's affair in 1820; Princess Lieven's letters from the King's court went to Metternich, the Congress's host.

Both were great political proceedings in which the House of Lords sat in judgment: Warren Hastings by impeachment in Westminster Hall (1788–95), the Queen by a Bill of Pains and Penalties in the Lords' own chamber, each with admission tickets, a packed gallery and a nation reading the evidence daily.
